analysis.one_liner: Caps court awards against makers of harmful products and shields medical-parts suppliers from most lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The House sent the bill to two committees on February 28, 1995, never brought it to a vote, and on March 8 pointed further action to a companion product liability bill (H.R. 956); it expired when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have set one federal rulebook for lawsuits over defective products, overriding state laws. It would have capped punitive damages, barred most claims filed more than 15 years after a product was sold, made each defendant pay only its own share of pain-and-suffering awards, and largely shielded companies that supply raw materials for medical implants from being sued. It never got a vote: the House referred it to two committees and then pointed further action to a companion bill.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers, product sellers, liability insurers, and companies that supply components for medical devices. They would gain predictable, lower liability costs: punitive awards capped, a 15-year cutoff on claims, no joint liability for pain-and-suffering, sanctions against plaintiffs who file weak pleadings, and near-immunity for biomaterials suppliers.

how_it_helps.text: Caps punitive damages at the greater of three times economic damages or $250,000, requires clear and convincing proof that the harm came from intentional or flagrantly indifferent conduct, and lets either side force a separate proceeding on punitive damages.

Bars most product liability lawsuits filed more than 15 years after a product was first sold or leased, unless the injured person received or is eligible for full compensation of medical expenses from some source.
Makes each defendant liable only for its own proportional share of noneconomic losses like pain and suffering, ending joint liability where one defendant could be forced to cover another's share.
Limits liability of product sellers to negligence, breach of warranty, or intentional wrongdoing, and lets sellers avoid strict liability that often applies under state law.

Gives biomaterials suppliers — companies that supply raw materials and parts for implanted medical devices — near-immunity unless they breached contract specifications, withheld material information, or knew of fraud, and requires plaintiffs who lose on a frivolous claim to pay the supplier's attorney fees.

Supporters argued in the bill's findings that unpredictable liability awards raise insurance costs and prices, drive products out of the national market, and threaten small businesses and US competitiveness.
Imposes sanctions, including attorney fees, on parties who file groundless pleadings in product liability cases in state court.

analysis.who_pays: People injured or killed by defective products. They would face a 15-year cutoff on claims, caps on punitive awards, and — if one responsible company cannot pay — the loss of the uncovered share of their pain-and-suffering damages. Residents of states with stronger consumer protections would lose those protections, because the bill overrides state law on the issues it covers.

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides state law nationwide, so a person injured in a state that offers broader recovery rights would lose them for any issue the federal rules cover.

Under the several-liability rule, a plaintiff collects pain-and-suffering damages only in proportion to each defendant's share of fault; if one defendant is insolvent or judgment-proof, the injured person absorbs the shortfall.

The punitive damages cap and the clear-and-convincing proof standard would sharply reduce or eliminate punitive awards in many cases where a company knowingly shipped a dangerous product, weakening the main financial deterrent beyond paying victims' actual losses.

The 15-year cutoff could bar claims for injuries that surface decades after exposure, though it carves out latent illnesses that ordinarily appear more than 15 years after first exposure and applies only when the claimant has or is eligible for full medical-expense compensation.
Frivolous-pleading sanctions and fee-shifting against biomaterials plaintiffs could deter people with legitimate but hard-to-prove claims from suing at all.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters made a real argument: businesses facing unpredictable jury awards raise prices, and some products leave the market. The bill's own findings claim those costs fall on consumers. But the design places nearly every limit on the injured side of the ledger — capping punishment, cutting off old claims, and shielding suppliers — while leaving the compensation guarantees in state workers' compensation and insurance systems untouched. For anyone seriously harmed by a defective product, the bill reduces recovery and predictability favors the companies being sued. It is a genuine trade-off, weighted toward product makers and insurers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in two House committees, never came up for a vote, and died when the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Hyde introduced the bill on February 28, 1995, and the House referred it to the Judiciary Committee and, in addition, the Commerce Committee.
On March 8, 1995, the House recorded no further action on this bill and pointed further action to H.R. 956, the House's main product liability reform bill of that Congress.
No vote was ever taken on the bill, and it expired with the Congress on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured people are better off, because the caps on punitive damages, the 15-year cutoff, and the biomaterials supplier shield never took effect, and state law continued to govern their claims. Manufacturers, sellers, and insurers lost the liability limits they sought in this Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and its single cosponsor were both Republicans, and federal product liability caps were a chiefly Republican priority in this Congress.

industries.note: The bill caps punitive damages, sets a 15-year cutoff on claims, and ends joint liability for pain-and-suffering, cutting the amounts companies pay when their products injure people. The savings come out of what injured consumers can recover.
Uniform federal rules and damage caps make payouts smaller and more predictable, which the bill's findings cite as a benefit to insurers. The cost falls on injured claimants rather than on insurers.

Title III gives companies that supply raw materials and parts for implanted medical devices near-immunity: plaintiffs must sue the device maker instead, meet narrow conditions to keep the supplier in the case, and pay the supplier's fees if a claim is ruled frivolous. People injured by implants lose access to a deep-pocket defendant.

Damage caps, claim cutoffs, and sanctions for weak pleadings reduce the value and number of product liability cases lawyers can take on contingency. Their business interest in this bill runs alongside injured people's interest in full recovery.
